narrative.overview:
Everydaypane’s product chrome (marketing site, household panel, family phone flows, sign-in, and outbound email) reads like a calm pane of kitchen glass: soft paper backgrounds, white panels, and a rare indigo accent that names the brand without shouting. Density stays practical — phone-first controls with comfortable tap targets — never gadget-dark neon or brochure-lifestyle cream.

The wall display is a separate visual layer: households pick themes (Aurora, Mist, Forest, …), fonts, radius, and glass opacity. That layer inherits glanceability and Canadian English, but not the marketing token sheet. New marketing or household UI extends this system; new wall chrome follows the active theme tokens in display.css, not these page tokens.
keyCharacteristics: Soft indigo brand on cool paper (#f6f7fb), not purple SaaS gradients
Manrope for display/wordmark; Inter for UI body
Flat panels with hairline borders; lift reserved for device mock and CTA banners
Wordmark: everydaypane with “pane” in brand blue

rules.name: The One Pane Rule
rules.body: Kitchen Indigo is the single brand voice on a screen; do not introduce a second primary accent for “interest.”

rules.name: The Paper Rule
rules.body: Page chrome sits on Cool Paper + Panel White with Hairline borders — not pure white full-bleed or cream lifestyle paper.

rules.name: The Wall Is Not This Sheet
rules.body: Do not apply marketing @theme colours to wall widgets; wall colour comes from the household’s chosen theme.

rules.name: The Wordmark Rule
rules.body: Product name is Everydaypane; the mark paints everydaypane with “pane” in Kitchen Indigo (or sun-on-indigo in inverted email headers). Do not invent EverydayPane / Everyday Pane in UI chrome.

rules.name: The Two-Family Rule
rules.body: Marketing/display voice = Manrope; operational UI body = Inter. Wall themes may swap Inter for Outfit, DM Sans, Literata, Space Grotesk — that choice stays on the wall.

rules.name: The Wall Floor Rule
rules.body: (design review, Melvin, 2026-11-26). The wall is read from two to three metres, so no text on /display/ goes under 16 px (--t-meta: labels, times, places, captions) and secondary lines stay at least 18 px (--t-small); primary rows aim for 28 px and up. Floors are max(… , var(--t-meta)) or a clamp() minimum, never a bare small em. Lists and short texts are sized for the whole tile and step down only when they overflow (fillTile in src/display/dom.ts); when a list still doesn't fit at the floor, the last rows are hidden whole (dropOverflow) rather than shrunk or cut in half. Tall, narrow tiles stack (agenda, countdowns) instead of squeezing a row. Exceptions: the dense month grid and map credits.

rules.name: The Phone Reach Rule
rules.body: Household and family controls keep ≥44px-class hit areas; do not shrink primary actions for desktop density alone.

rules.name: The Flat-By-Default Rule
rules.body: Surfaces stay flat at rest. Shadows appear for device theatre or primary persuasion — not under every admin card.

rules.name: The Soft Corner Rule
rules.body: Prefer xl/2xl radii from the token scale; avoid sharp rectangles and full-pill primary buttons (pills are for indicators, not CTAs).

rules.name: The Shared Utility Rule
rules.body: Prefer btn / btn-primary / btn-ghost / field / card from globals.css over one-off Tailwind stacks for the same jobs.

dos: Do keep Kitchen Indigo as the sole primary accent on product chrome.
Do set everydaypane with “pane” in brand blue on light surfaces.
Do use Manrope for marketing/display voice and Inter for operational body UI.
Do honour prefers-reduced-motion (disable site-rise; solid states for alarms on the wall).
Do use Canadian English in UI copy (colour, centre, favourite).

Do write names in Title Case (headings, tabs, buttons, labels, options, widget titles, wall status chips) and sentences in sentence case (hints, errors, empty states, emails, body copy); titleCase in src/lib/titleCase.ts has the rules (Melvin, 2026-11-26).
donts: Don't restyle the wall with marketing @theme tokens — wall themes own that surface.
Don't invent purple-on-white SaaS gradients, cream/serif lifestyle brochure looks, or dense broadsheet layouts for product chrome.
Don't put personal family photos in OG, marketing, or template proof — use public/templates/ / feature widget samples.
Don't “fix” wall pinch-zoom locks; that exception is product policy, not a design bug.
Don't add a second email template system — reuse src/lib/email.ts chrome.
